sentences.text: Diamantinasaurus was a medium-sized titanosaurian that reached lengths of 16 meters and weighed up to 25 tonnes.
Fossil remains include nearly the entire right forelimb, the left humerus, and the left first metacarpal, alongside hindlimb bones such as the ilium, pubes, ischia, and the right leg.
The shoulder blade features an outwardly rotated glenoid articulation and a robust, round cross-section, traits unique among somphospondylans.
The upper rim of the ilium is fractured, revealing tiny internal cavities similar to those seen in Alamosaurus and other relatives.
A 2023 study revealed a more complete skull measuring 50 centimeters in length.
Preserved stomach contents show the animal ate conifers, seed ferns, and flowering plants using a bulk-feeding strategy.
Fossils of the predator Australovenator were found at the same location, sharing the environment with turtles, crocodiles, and fish.
The species D. matildae was first named in 2009 by Scott Hocknull and colleagues in the journal PLoS ONE.
The holotype specimen was uncovered during four seasons of digging near Winton in Queensland, Australia.
Additional specimens, cataloged as AODF 0603 and AODF 0604, were also described by the same team in that year.
In 2025, researchers detailed fossilized gut contents from the subadult specimen AODF 0888.
This large quadrupedal herbivore moved on four legs.
Its skull shape resembled brachiosaurids more than derived titanosaurs, hinting at a close link to the Argentinian Sarmientosaurus.
The skeleton possessed at least five, and perhaps six, sacral vertebrae.
Evidence from the gut suggests the animal relied on fermentation and gut microflora to digest its plant diet.
Its bones are set apart from other sauropods by their overall sturdiness and multiple specific characteristics.
A 2014 study placed the genus as a lithostrotian in a relatively advanced position within Titanosauria.
Later analyses by Gorscak and O'Connor (2019) recovered it as a saltasaurid via parsimony, though Bayesian methods placed it just outside that family.
The parent group for this genus is Diamantinasauria.
Diamantinasaurus lived in Australia during the early Late Cretaceous, roughly 94 million years ago, within the middle to upper Winton Formation.
The estimated time range spans from 100.5 to 89.8 million years ago, covering the Cenomanian to Turonian stages.
Poropat et al. (2014) hypothesized that the lack of carpal bones in fossils means they were genuinely absent in life, a view similar to Opisthocoelicaudia and Alamosaurus.
The same authors suggested based on Diamantinasaurus that all titanosaurs had ossified phalanges, contrasting with earlier studies.
A 2011 study described the smallest positively identified titanosaur embryo, which shares the most features with Diamantinasaurus and Rapetosaurus.
